question: A 63-year-old woman with a previous diagnosis of rheumatoid arthritis and Sjogren syndrome was referred for a second opinion. She has had a known chronic idiopathic pericardial effusion for about a year and has dealt with intermittent chest pain ever since. She underwent 2 diagnostic pericardiocenteses, but the fluid returned each time. She also has used empiric anti-inflammatory therapies with NSAIDs and colchicine without significant changes in the size of the pericardial effusion. The etiological testing was negative. At this visit, she is still complaining of pain in her chest but has no evidence of distended neck veins. An ECG shows sinus rhythm with low QRS voltages. What will be the procedure of choice that would be both therapeutic and diagnostic?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Chronic idiopathic pericardial effusion -> recurrent fluid accumulation -> failed response to pericardiocentesis -> 70% CHAIN: Intermittent chest pain -> no resolution with NSAIDs and colchicine -> 60% CHAIN: Negative etiological testing -> ruling out infectious or autoimmune causes -> 80% CHAIN: Sinus rhythm with low QRS voltages on ECG -> possible pericardial constriction -> 70% CHAIN: Empiric anti-inflammatory therapies ineffective -> consideration for pericardial window -> 75% CHAIN: Pericardial window -> both therapeutic and diagnostic for chronic idiopathic pericardial effusion -> 70%
enhanced_information: For a 63-year-old woman with chronic idiopathic pericardial effusion and recurrent fluid accumulation despite failed pericardiocentesis, consideration of a pericardial window is appropriate. This procedure is both therapeutic and diagnostic, especially when empirical anti-inflammatory therapies have been ineffective. The presence of sinus rhythm with low QRS voltages on ECG raises concern for possible pericardial constriction, further supporting the choice of a pericardial window.
analysis: Given the patient's history of chronic idiopathic pericardial effusion with recurrent fluid accumulation despite failed pericardiocentesis and ineffective anti-inflammatory therapies, along with ECG findings suggestive of possible pericardial constriction, the most appropriate procedure that is both therapeutic and diagnostic would be a pericardial window. This procedure can help drain the effusion, relieve symptoms, and provide tissue for further evaluation.
